title: Success metrics
text: A strong answer names at least one primary metric tied to the user outcome, says how it is measured, and ideally adds a guardrail metric. Vague goals such as 'improve satisfaction' do not count.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: User segmentation
text: A strong answer identifies who the users are in a B2B setting (buyer, admin, end user) and which segment it prioritizes and why. Treating all users as one group is a gap.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: Problem framing
text: A strong answer clarifies the problem before proposing solutions: asks or states assumptions, defines the pain point, and checks the root cause. Jumping straight to features is a gap.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: Prioritization
text: A strong answer uses an explicit logic (impact, effort, strategic fit, evidence) to choose among options and says what it would not do. A list of ideas without a choice is a gap.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: Tradeoffs and risks
text: A strong answer names what is given up by the chosen path, the main risks, and how it would detect that it is wrong. Presenting the plan as risk free is a gap.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: Staying on topic
text: The answer must address the question asked. An answer about a different problem, or generic career talk that never touches the scenario, is off topic.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team

title: Minimum substance
text: An empty answer or one with only a few words cannot be assessed and counts as too short.
source: Team starter rubric, to be rewritten by the team
